ca_electromagnetic_crag.blurb: A small, steep conglomerate wall on the Acton hillside above Soledad Canyon Road, in the Angeles National Forest northeast of the Los Angeles Basin. Almost everything here is bolted, short and overhanging, roughly 50 to 65 feet, with the bulk of the lines in the 5.12 range plus a couple of 5.11s and a few 5.13s. One trad crack and top-rope option sits among them. Unlike the loose domes nearby, the rock here is clean and fairly solid. The face stays shaded until early afternoon, which makes it a good bet for most of the year but too warm in summer. Expect a steep half-hour hike, then power lines overhead and wide views down the valley.

ca_hoodie_the.blurb: The Hoodie is a dark, steep wall facing east on Fairview Mountain, in the high desert near Apple Valley. It is the first formation you meet on the canyon trail heading toward Middle Earth, about a ten-minute walk uphill, so it works as a quick stop or a warm-up for the bigger valley beyond. Nearly all of it is bolted sport climbing, from a single 5.9 through a cluster of 5.10s, mostly 5.11s, and one 5.12 at the top end, plus a single easy boulder problem. It is a small crag with only about ten lines, and morning sun is the likely draw.

ca_iguana_the.blurb: The Iguana is an intricate pile of boulders in the Galapagos, one of Joshua Tree's more remote corners, on the desert flats west of Geology Tour Road and southwest of Ryan Mountain. Getting here takes a long cross-country walk of more than an hour, so you will likely have it to yourself. Eleven routes, nearly all trad, with one bolted line: a couple of beginner-level pitches, a handful of 5.8s, a few 5.9s and 5.10s, and one 5.11. The best-known line is a crack in the 5.10 range, and finger and hand cracks dominate. It suits a self-sufficient party with a standard rack.

ca_locals_only_rock.blurb: Locals Only Rock is one of about ten formations at Benton Crags, a remote, high-elevation spot in the Eastern Sierra with broad views toward the high peaks. It is the closest rock to the parking area, the first one you reach heading east from the lot. Most of its eleven routes are trad, a few can be top-roped, and the difficulty stays friendly: mostly 5.6 through 5.9, with one easy low-angle ridge and a single 5.10. The namesake 5.6 is the popular line. Bring a standard rack and be ready to rappel or downclimb the class 4 terrain on the north side.

ca_lost_horse_wall_left_side.blurb: The left end of Lost Horse Wall in Joshua Tree is the portion nearest the road, at about 4,100 feet. It faces west, so afternoon sun hits it. The ten or so routes are mostly trad with two bolted lines, and they skew hard for the park: one 5.9, four 5.10s, and six 5.11s, with the better-known lines around 5.10c to 5.11c. Climbing mixes technical cracks with face moves, on a short approach. This is more of a stop for intermediate and advanced climbers than a first-timer wall, and a standard rack with attention to cam sizes is recommended.
